title: Converting Concentration Units
short: Use the solution's density to switch between molarity, molality and mass percent.
trouble: Students treat the solution's volume in milliliters as the mass of solvent in grams, which fails for concentrated solutions.

blocks.html: Bottles of concentrated acid are labeled with mass percent and density; a recipe asks for molarity; a freezing-point problem needs molality. Molality, Mole Fraction and Parts per Million defined each one, and Density is the bridge between mass and volume that lets you switch.

Pick a convenient amount and split it into solute and solvent. For molarity, take 1 L of solution: its mass is $1000 \times d$ grams. For mass percent or molality, take 100 g of solution or 1 kg of solvent. Then find moles of solute, mass of solvent and volume of solution, and divide as each unit asks.

Concentration is a ratio, so it doesn't depend on how much solution you imagine. Choosing 1 L or 100 g makes the arithmetic easy. The only extra fact needed is how mass and volume are related for this solution, its density. Molarity has volume of solution on the bottom; molality has mass of solvent; so going between them you must account for the mass of the solute itself, which is large in concentrated solutions.

blocks.name: ch-convert
blocks.cap: One liter of concentrated hydrochloric acid weighs 1180 g; 37.0% of that is HCl, about 12 mol: the bottle is 12 M.

blocks.title: Mass percent to molarity
blocks.q: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is 37.0% HCl by mass and has a density of $1.18\ \text{g/mL}$. Find its molarity (HCl $36.46\ \text{g/mol}$).

blocks.title: Mass percent to molality
blocks.q: Find the molality of the same 37.0% HCl.
steps: Take 100.0 g of solution: 37.0 g HCl and $100.0 - 37.0 = 63.0\ \text{g}$ of water.
Molality: $1.015/0.0630 = 16.1\ \text{mol/kg}$. Much larger than 12.0 M: in a concentrated solution, a liter of solution holds much less than a kilogram of water.

blocks.title: Molarity to molality
blocks.q: A $1.00\ \text{M}$ NaCl solution has a density of $1.040\ \text{g/mL}$. Find its molality.
steps: 1.000 L of solution: $1040\ \text{g}$, containing $1.00\ \text{mol} = 58.44\ \text{g}$ of NaCl.

blocks.html: Treating the volume of solution in milliliters as the mass of solvent in grams, so that 1 L of 12 M HCl seems to hold 1000 g of water. It holds only about 743 g (1180 g of solution minus 436.6 g of HCl). The shortcut "molarity ≈ molality" works only for dilute water solutions. Check: always subtract the solute's mass to get the solvent's.
